name: Vanchinathar Temple, Srivanchiyam
deity: Shiva as Vanchinathar, with the goddess Mangalambikai
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung in the Tevaram
summary: Srivanchiyam, near Tiruvarur, is one of the few temples in the land where Yama, the god of death, has a shrine of his own and a central place in worship. Shiva is enshrined here as Vanchinathar, a Paadal Petra Sthalam sung in the Tevaram, with the goddess Mangalambikai. By tradition Yama himself did penance here and the lord granted that those who die at this kshetra be freed from the fear of death and the round of rebirth — making Srivanchiyam a revered place for rites concerning the departed.

sections.history: Srivanchiyam is an ancient Shaiva village-temple in the Tiruvarur country, counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams and hymned in the Tevaram. The stone temple reflects Chola-period building with later additions; the sanctum enshrines a lingam worshipped as Vanchinathar. What sets the temple apart in the long Tevaram tradition is the prominence given to Yama, whose shrine and role in worship are unusual among Shiva temples and have shaped the kshetra's special association with death and release.
sections.architecture: The temple is laid out on the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, pillared halls and the sanctum of Vanchinathar, with the goddess Mangalambikai in her own shrine. Its distinctive feature is the shrine of Yama, given a place of honour rarely seen elsewhere. Within the complex is the sacred tank known as Gupta Ganga, 'the hidden Ganga,' which tradition holds to carry the secret presence of the river goddess, and which pilgrims revere for its purifying waters.
sections.legends: The temple's defining tradition concerns Yama, the god of death. By one account Yama performed penance here to be freed from a curse, and Shiva, pleased, granted that those who end their lives at this kshetra be released from the terror of death and from the cycle of rebirth. The sthala-purana also tells of Surya regaining his lost radiance here after the episode of Daksha's sacrifice, and of the Ganga leaving a portion of her power in the Gupta Ganga tank. These stories together mark Srivanchiyam as a place of purification and peaceful passage.
sections.festivals: The most prominent festival is Masi Magam, in the Tamil month of Masi, when the processional image of the lord is carried through the streets on the mount of Yama — a usage found at few other temples. The Shaiva observances of Maha Shivaratri and Pradosham are also kept, and the temple is much visited for rites performed on behalf of ancestors and the recently departed.
sections.experience: Srivanchiyam carries a quiet gravity drawn from its association with death and liberation. Families come to perform rites for the departed and to pray at the rare shrine of Yama, bathing in the Gupta Ganga before worship. For many it is a place that turns the fear of mortality toward the hope of release, and the temple holds that solemn consolation at its heart.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Srivanchiyam is in Tiruvarur district, about 18 km from Tiruvarur and close to Nannilam; the nearest rail heads are Tiruvarur and Nannilam, with local buses and taxis to the village.
